newsitem.title: UK: CalPERS outlines UK, French governance proposals.
newsitem.headline: CalPERS outlines UK, French governance proposals.

text.p: The California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS), the largest public pension fund in the U.S., on Thursday formally presented its corporate governance principles for companies in which it invests in Britain and France.

CalPERS, which has $3.7 billion invested in Britain and $1.9 billion in France and is a particularly active shareholder in terms of corporate governance and seeking boardroom changes, said in a statement that the principles build on six concepts it had identified as fundamental to free and fair markets.

These included director accountability to shareholders, transparent markets, equitable treatment for all shareholders, easy and efficient voting methods, codes of best practices that clearly define the director-shareholder relationship, and long-term corporate vision which "at its core emphasises shareholder value".

In Britain, CalPERS is calling for existing corporate governance codes to be the minimum benchmark and outlined its intention to exercise its rights as a share owner, urging other shareholders to do the same.

CalPERS suggests changes to ensure directors are fully accountable and independent, including the regular election of all directors, a separate chairman and chief executive with the chairman an independet director, a majority of independent directors, confidential voting and improved access for shareholders to present resolutions.

In France, CalPERS is endorsing the Vienot code drawn up in 1995 as the minimum benchmark and recommends a one-share, one-vote capital structure, an end to cross shareholding, the regular election of all directors and a greater disclosure of executive pay.

"France needs to begin meeting market expectations and requirements in order to coninue to attract capital from insitutional investors," CalPERS' investment committee chairman Charles Valdes said. "Better disclosure and a greater focus on the role of shareholders when defining the corporations' interests are key to continuing the capital flow," he said.

CalPERS board of administration president William Crist said the principles would "serve as a tool to assist us in monitoring our investments in these countries while pursuing better corporate governance for the companies in which the fund invests".
The CalPERS move, to be presented by CalPERS' chief lawyer Kayla Gillan at a news conference in London on Thursday, adds to a widespread debate over corporate governence in recent years.
Earlier this week, the former British post office pension fund Hermes Investment Management outlined its own proposals for Britain, which also stressed non-executive independence and accountability.
